newsitem.title: USA: GM sets base minivan prices above Ford, Chrysler.
newsitem.headline: GM sets base minivan prices above Ford, Chrysler.

text.p: General Motors Corp. said Thursday that prices for its trio of new minivans will start at $20,495, significantly higher than competing models from Chrysler Corp. and Ford Motor Co.

The highly anticipated vehicles -- the Chevrolet Venture, Pontiac Trans Sport and Oldsmobile Silhouette -- replace GM's slow-selling, plastic-bodied APV minivans and are beginning to trickle into dealerships.

The $20,495 price buys a three-door, short-wheelbase Chevrolet Venture minivan, and prices range to $26,805 for the largest, most luxurious Oldsmobile Silhouette. The prices include a $570 destination and delivery charge.
Chevrolet said it expects its volume leader to be the Venture long-wheelbase LS model equipped with a left-side sliding door, which will carry popular options and a price of $24,319.
The prices surprised analysts, who had expected GM to undercut Ford's and Chrysler's pricing in an effort to establish itself as the value leader in minivans.
For 1997, Chrysler's minivans start at $17,815, while Ford's Windstar van gets a new lower price of $18,995.
Chrysler, which dominates the U.S. minivan market, has priced its volume leader, the long-wheelbase, four-door Caravan SE, at $21,930 and its top-of-the line Town & Country LXi at $32,045.
Analysts said the pricing strategy makes it clear that GM doesn't plan to serve the low end of the minivan market.

"This pricing is going to hurt them," said Wes Brown, an auto analyst for CSM Forecasting in Farmington Hills, Mich. "We are going to have to lower our forecast for those vehicles and for their plant."
GM is building the vans and a sibling for Europe -- the Opel Sintra -- at its Doraville, Ga., assembly plant, which is capable of building about 240,000 vehicles annually.
GM's marketing chief, Ronald Zarrella, defended the decision Thursday, saying that the new minivans are priced the way most people buy them.
"You can't look at base prices. Nobody buys that," he said after a speech in New York. "It's not meaningful."
He also said that in the mid-level and higher price ranges, the GM vans are competitive, and in some cases, cheaper than Chrysler's offerings.
The GM vans also offer a powerful standard engine -- a 3.4-litre, 24-valve V-6 that produces 180 horsepower. Chrysler's cheapest minivan has a four-cylinder engine and Ford's has a less powerful V-6.
Brown said the GM minivans are a vast improvement over their long-snouted predecessors, but doubts that consumers will be willing to pay premium prices for them.
"They don't break any ground and aren't as stylish as the Chrysler vans," he added.
